answer: I'd like to talk about a performance that completely changed how I think about music. A time I was genuinely impressed was when I went to a large classical music festival in Dhaka with my elder sister and her husband a few years ago. I had always enjoyed music, but I had never experienced anything on that scale in person. The festival ran through the night in a huge open-air venue, with thousands of people sitting on the ground and listening in near silence. We had brought a thin mat and a flask of tea, like most of the people around us. From the moment the performance began, I was completely [[captivated]]. The sheer skill of the musicians, a sitar player and a tabla player responding to each other in perfect harmony, was absolutely [[remarkable]]. What impressed me most was the emotion they managed to convey purely through their instruments, with no words at all. The sound was so rich and powerful that I felt it [[resonate]] in my chest. It was a genuinely [[mesmerising]] experience, quite unlike listening to a recording on my phone. I came away with a whole new appreciation for the years of discipline behind such a performance, since musicians like that often train from childhood. Honestly, it left me feeling deeply [[moved]], and it reminded me of the extraordinary things humans can achieve through dedication. By the time we left, the sun was coming up, and I was tired but completely inspired. I have been eager to attend more live performances ever since.

followUps.q: What kind of music do you usually listen to?
followUps.answer: Mostly Bengali songs, both old classics and some modern bands, and a bit of English pop. I listen while walking by the river in the evening, which is probably my favourite time for music.

followUps.q: Have you ever wanted to learn a musical instrument?
followUps.answer: Yes, the tabla, after that festival. I never actually started, though, because I didn't have the time. Perhaps one day, when life is a little less busy, I will finally give it a try.

note: Western orchestra replaced by an all-night classical music festival in Dhaka (sitar and tabla), with his elder sister; marked 'resonate'.
